lessons.title: Welcome to FE102!
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
FE102's goal is to build a small React web app with a list, search/filter, and real data from an API, like a simple item browser.

KEY IDEAS
1. Hello, React: get a first React app running.
2. Building Components: reusable pieces of UI.
3. UIs that react: the UI changes when data or inputs change.
4. Apps that talk to the world: fetch data from an API and show it in a searchable list.

KEY POINTS
- The course has 4 units, in the order above.
- The final app combines all four: components, state, and fetched data.

lessons.title: What is React, and why do we need it?
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Plain JavaScript is imperative: you tell the browser each step ("find #followers, change its text"). React is declarative: you describe what the UI should look like for your data, and React updates the page when the data changes.

KEY IDEAS
1. Imperative (plain JS + DOM): "When X happens, find element Y and update it." You must remember every place that needs updating.
2. Declarative (React): "This UI always shows followers and isFollowing." You change the data; React redraws the right parts.
3. React's core promise: UI = a function of data.

STEPS
Plain JS follower button:
1. Button is clicked.
2. document.querySelector("#followers") finds the element.
3. Change its .textContent by hand.

React follower button:
1. Button is clicked.
2. Update the followers value.
3. React re-renders the component with the new value.

KEY POINTS
- Plain JS: you update the numbers on the page yourself.
- React: the numbers update automatically when the data changes.
- React fits pages where values change often: counters, stats, dashboards.

lessons.title: Meet the terminal
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
The terminal is a text panel for giving your computer commands. In VS Code it opens with Ctrl + ` (Cmd + ` on Mac) or View → Terminal, and runs PowerShell on Windows.

KEY IDEAS
1. The prompt shows the shell and the current folder, then waits for a command.
2. Prompt visible = ready to type. No prompt and text still printing = a command is still running.
3. Ctrl + C stops a running command (a dev server, a watcher, ping -t). The prompt then comes back.
4. The VS Code terminal is the same shell as the system terminal, just docked next to your code and opened in your project folder.

CODE
```text
PS C:\Users\Tunacancode\Desktop\my-first-html-page>
PS = PowerShell
C:\Users\...\my-first-html-page = current folder (working directory)
>  = ready for a command
```

```text
pwd        # print working directory: where am I?
ls         # list files and folders here
cd name    # go into the folder "name"
cd ..      # go up one folder
```

KEY POINTS
- PowerShell accepts pwd, ls and cd as aliases for its own commands.
- Before typing, check that the prompt is showing.
- Ctrl + C is the standard way to stop something that keeps running.

lessons.title: Install Node.js and npm
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser, in the terminal. It has no DOM (no page to draw on) and is used for tools, scripts and builds, including the tools behind React. npm, the package tool, comes with Node.

KEY IDEAS
1. JavaScript runs in two places: the browser (has the DOM, shows pages) and Node.js (runs in the terminal, no DOM).
2. Node is the engine React's dev server and build tools run on.
3. npm installs and manages packages; it is installed together with Node.

STEPS
Check the setup:
1. node -v prints the Node version (here v24.15.0).
2. npm -v prints the npm version (here 11.12.1).
3. Make hello.js with one console.log line.
4. From that folder, run node hello.js.
5. Seeing both versions and "Hello from Node" with no errors means the toolchain works.

CODE
```javascript
// hello.js
console.log('Hello from Node');
```

```powershell
node -v
npm -v
node hello.js
# Hello from Node
```

If PowerShell blocks npm scripts:
```powershell
Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser
# answer Y when asked
```

KEY POINTS
- node file.js runs a file with Node, not the browser.
- Node has no document or window, because there is no page.

NOTE
Set-ExecutionPolicy with -Scope CurrentUser only changes the setting for your own user, so it doesn't need an Admin window. Running it as Admin works too.

lessons.title: Your first npm project
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
An npm project is a folder with a package.json file. package.json lists the project's settings and the packages it needs, node_modules/ holds the installed package code, and package-lock.json records the exact versions installed.

KEY IDEAS
1. package.json fields:
   - name: the project name
   - version: the project version (1.0.0 by default)
   - main: the entry file (for example index.js)
   - scripts: named shortcuts, run with npm run <name>
   - dependencies: packages the app needs when it runs
   - devDependencies: tools needed only while developing
2. node_modules/: the real files of every installed package. You don't edit them.
3. package-lock.json: written by npm. Stores exact versions and hashes so installs are the same on another machine or later.
4. Local install: listed in this project's package.json, lives in its node_modules/, usable with require()/import.
5. Global install (-g): a command-line tool that works from any folder; not listed in package.json.

STEPS
1. Make a folder (for example first-npm-game-ui) and open it in VS Code.
2. npm init -y creates package.json.
3. npm install chalk@4 adds chalk to dependencies, creates node_modules/, and writes package-lock.json.
4. Use it in index.js with require('chalk').
5. node index.js runs it.

CODE
```json
"dependencies": {
  "chalk": "^4.1.2"
}
```

```javascript
// index.js
const chalk = require('chalk');
console.log(chalk.green('Player joined the game!'));
console.log(chalk.red('Player took damage!'));
```

```text
npm init -y                   -> create package.json
npm install <pkg>             -> add to dependencies
npm install --save-dev <pkg>  -> add to devDependencies (example: nodemon)
npm uninstall <pkg>           -> remove it and update node_modules and the lockfile
npm install -g <pkg>          -> install a global tool (example: cowsay)
```

KEY POINTS
- dependencies = needed at run time (chalk, used by index.js).
- devDependencies = needed only while developing (nodemon, which restarts the app when files change).
- ^4.1.2 means "4.1.2 or any newer 4.x version".

NOTE
chalk version 5 and later only works with import, not require(). This code uses require('chalk'), so version 4 is the right one.

lessons.title: Create your React project with Vite
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Browsers understand plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, but not JSX or bare imports like import React from 'react'. Vite sits in the middle: it turns React code into browser-ready JavaScript and serves it on localhost.

KEY IDEAS
1. Build tool: reads src/main.jsx and src/App.jsx, turns JSX and imports into plain JavaScript, and bundles it.
2. Dev server: npm run dev serves the app at http://localhost:5173/. The terminal stays busy until you press Ctrl + C.
3. Hot Module Replacement (HMR): save a file and only that module is rebuilt; the page updates without a full refresh.

STEPS
1. Move out of system folders: cd $HOME, then pwd to check (should be C:\Users\YourName).
2. mkdir my-react-test, then cd my-react-test.
3. npm create vite@latest . (the dot means "in this folder"). Choose React, then JavaScript.
4. npm install.
5. npm run dev, and look for Local: http://localhost:5173/.
6. Open that address in the browser.
7. Edit visible text in src/App.jsx and save. The page updates on its own.
8. Ctrl + C in that terminal stops the server.

If the site can't be reached or breaks:
1. pwd: are you in the project folder?
2. Is npm run dev still running? Start it again if not.
3. Open http://localhost:5173/ only after the server is running.
4. If an edit crashed the app, read the error, look for a missing closing tag or stray characters, fix, and save.

KEY POINTS
- Vite's three jobs: build tool, dev server, HMR.
- The dev server only works while its terminal is running it.

NOTE
Vite isn't only for React. It also works with Vue, Svelte and plain JavaScript. React was picked in the setup prompt.

lessons.title: Meet JSX
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS JSX is HTML-like markup written inside JavaScript, usually inside a component's return ( ... ). It looks like HTML but has a few strict rules. KEY IDEAS 1. One root element: everything returned must be inside one outer element, such as a
or a fragment <>.... 2. className instead of class, because class is a JavaScript keyword. 3. Self-close tags with no content: ,
, . 4. Opening and closing tags must match exactly, including capitalization. CODE Wrong (two roots): ```jsx return (

Paused

Game is paused

); ``` Right (one root): ```jsx return (

Paused

); ``` ```jsx

``` Wrong: ```jsx

``` Full example: ```jsx function App() { return (

lessons.title: Embedding values in JSX
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS Curly braces { } in JSX insert the result of a JavaScript expression into the UI. An expression is anything that produces a value: a variable, math, a function call, or string building. KEY IDEAS 1. Allowed inside { }: expressions, like {score}, {hp + 5}, {formatScore(score)}, {"HP: " + hp}. 2. Operators like &&, || and ? : are expressions too, so they work inside { }. 3. Not allowed: statements, like if, for, while, switch and try/catch. 4. Don't change values inside { } (for example {level = level + 1}). Braces are for what to show, not for changing state. CODE ```jsx const score = 120; const hp = 35; function formatScore(score) { return score.toString().padStart(6, "0"); }

Score: {score}

// Score: 120

HP: {hp + 5}

// HP: 40

Score: {formatScore(score)}

// Score: 000120

{"HP: " + hp}

// HP: 35 ``` Wrong: ```jsx

{if (hp > 0) "Alive"}

``` Right (the expression version of that if): ```jsx

{hp > 0 ? "Alive" : "Down"}

``` KEY POINTS - Ask: "Inside these braces, am I only computing a value to show?" If yes, it belongs there. - Branching with if or looping with for happens outside the JSX, or with ? : and .map().

lessons.title: Your first component
Reading React errors
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
React errors show up in two places. Build-time errors (red Vite overlay and terminal) mean the app never started, usually because of JSX or syntax. Runtime errors (browser Console, no overlay, often a blank screen) mean the app built but crashed while running.

KEY IDEAS
1. Terminal (Vite): shows whether Vite could build the app.
2. Red Vite overlay in the browser: shows the message, the file, and line:column (for example src/App.jsx:14:7).
3. Browser DevTools → Console: shows runtime errors.
4. Common messages:
   - "X is not defined": the name doesn't exist in this file or scope. Check spelling and the declaration.
   - "X is not a function": X exists but isn't a function. Check what value X really holds.
   - "Expected corresponding JSX closing tag for '<div>'": a tag is missing or doesn't match.

STEPS
1. Red overlay? Open the file and line it names, fix it, and save.
2. No overlay? Check the terminal for a new red error and read its file and line.
3. Still nothing? Open DevTools → Console and read the first red error.
4. Use its file and line to find the code and fix it.

CODE
```jsx
const hp = 100;
return <HealthBar value={health} />; // health is not defined

return <HealthBar value={hp} />;     // fixed: matches the variable name
```

KEY POINTS
- Overlay = build-time. Console only = runtime.
- Always read the first error first; later errors are often caused by it.

lessons.title: Tour your React project
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS A Vite React project has one real HTML page (index.html) with one mount point,
. src/main.jsx finds #root and renders into it. App.jsx is the root component, and other components live in src/components/. KEY IDEAS 1. index.html (project root): the only real HTML page; holds
. 2. src/main.jsx: the JavaScript entry. Imports StrictMode, createRoot, App and the CSS, then renders into #root. 3. src/App.jsx: the root component; the top of the UI tree. 4. src/components/: extra components used inside App, for example MiniMap.jsx. 5. public/: static files only (icons, images) that the browser fetches directly. No React code. 6. src/: all React code and styles. Vite bundles it. STEPS How the page gets on screen: 1. The browser loads index.html. 2. index.html contains
. 3. main.jsx finds #root and renders inside . 4. App.jsx returns JSX. 5. React draws that JSX inside #root. CODE ```jsx // src/main.jsx createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render( ) ``` ```jsx // in App.jsx import MiniMap from './components/MiniMap.jsx' ``` KEY POINTS - id must be unique on the page; React uses id="root" as its one mount point. - className can be reused on many elements and is used for styling. - StrictMode adds extra checks during development only.

lessons.title: Props: data into a component
Conditional rendering
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS Conditional rendering shows different JSX, or nothing, depending on a condition. Use && for "show it or nothing" and ? : for "always show one of two". KEY IDEAS 1. {condition && }: if the condition is truthy, show the JSX; if falsy, show nothing. 2. {condition ? A : B}: if true, show A; otherwise show B. 3. Falsy values: 0, "", null, undefined, false, NaN. Everything else is truthy. 4. The 0 trap: {0 &&

Hi

} evaluates to 0, and React puts 0 on the screen. React shows numbers, but skips false, null and undefined. CODE ```jsx {role &&

{role}

} // nothing when role is "" {enemyIsBoss && Boss}

{isOnline ? "Online" : "Offline"}

{isLowHealth ? "Low Health!" : "Healthy"}

``` The 0 trap and the fix: ```jsx {potions &&

Potions: {potions}

} // potions = 0 shows "0" {potions > 0 &&

Potions: {potions}

} // always true or false ``` KEY POINTS - Optional line that can disappear → &&. - Always one of two states → ? :. - When 0 is a real value, compare (potions > 0) instead of using the number itself.

lessons.title: Render a list from an array
Keys: how React tracks list items
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
A key tells React which list item is which. It is the item's identity, not its position. Use a stable, unique id (key={profile.id}), not the array index.

KEY IDEAS
1. Good key: an id that never changes for that item.
2. Index as key is tied to the slot (0, 1, 2...). Adding, removing or reordering items shifts the indexes.
3. When indexes shift, React can attach one item's state (typed text, animation, HP) to a different item.
4. With ids, React can match "id 4" to the same item even after sorting, filtering or reversing.
5. Keys only need to be unique among siblings in the same list. Two different lists can both use 1, 2, 3.

CODE
```jsx
<ProfileCard
  key={profile.id}
  name={profile.name}
  role={profile.role}
  isOnline={profile.isOnline}
/>
```

KEY POINTS
- Missing or repeated keys cause this console warning: Each child in a list should have a unique "key" prop.
- The key goes on the outermost element returned inside map.
- key is used by React and is not passed to the component as a prop.

lessons.title: Composing components
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS Composing components means building small components and nesting them inside bigger ones. The parent is the component whose JSX contains the others. Anything written between a component's opening and closing tags is passed to it as a special prop called children. KEY IDEAS 1. Parent: the component that renders other components in its JSX. If App renders many ProfileCards, App is the parent. 2. Child: a component written between and . 3. Nesting comes from the tags, not the indentation. on one line works the same; spaces are only for readability. 4. children: React's built-in prop that holds everything between the tags. It can be any mix of components and HTML elements, in order. 5. A layout component (CardGrid, ItemGrid, MenuGrid) doesn't care what its children are. It renders {children} wherever they should appear. 6. The prop must be named children. A name like buttons or items would be empty unless you pass it yourself as buttons={...}. lessons.title: Default and named exports
Styling React components
Challenge: build a reusable list UI
State with useState
How re-renders work
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
React re-renders a component when its state changes. Each render sees a fixed snapshot of state. Regular let/const variables inside the component start over on every render and never cause a re-render.

KEY IDEAS
1. Causes a re-render: calling a state setter, like setCount(count + 1).
2. Does not cause a re-render: changing a let/const, console.log, math.
3. State is remembered across renders; regular variables are recreated each render.
4. Snapshot rule: during one handler, count doesn't change. setCount(count + 1) only changes what count will be on the next render.

STEPS
One click, in order:
1. React calls the component (render).
2. The user clicks; the handler runs.
3. The handler calls the setter; React schedules an update.
4. React calls the component again with the new state.

CODE
```jsx
const [count, setCount] = useState(0); // state
let clicks = 0;                        // regular variable
```

One click, starting at count = 0:
```text
RENDER:        count = 0  clicks = 0
HANDLER START: count = 0  clicks = 0
HANDLER END:   count = 0  clicks = 1
RENDER:        count = 1  clicks = 0
```

```text
Before setCount -> count = X
After setCount  -> count is still X (in this handler)
Next render     -> count = X + 1
```

KEY POINTS
- setState → re-render. State persists. let/const resets.
- The new state value appears on the next render, not on the next line.

CORRECTION
StrictMode (development only) calls your component function twice, so render logs can appear twice. It also runs effects twice on mount. It does not run event handlers twice, so one click runs the handler once. If a handler's logs appear twice, check whether the log is inside a state updater function (those are called twice) or whether the click happened twice.

lessons.title: Updates that depend on the previous state
Updating objects and arrays in state
Controlled inputs
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
A controlled input gets its text from state and updates state on every keystroke, so React always knows what's in it. An uncontrolled input lets the browser keep the text, and you read it later, for example on submit.

KEY IDEAS
1. Controlled: value={state} plus onChange that calls the setter with event.target.value. React is the single source of truth.
2. Uncontrolled: no value prop (optionally defaultValue for the starting text). The browser updates the text as you type.
3. Use controlled inputs for live previews, validation, character counters, or syncing with other UI.
4. Use uncontrolled inputs when only the final value matters.

CODE
Controlled:
```jsx
const [value, setValue] = useState('');

<input
  type="text"
  value={value}
  onChange={e => setValue(e.target.value)}
/>
```

Uncontrolled:
```jsx
<input type="text" />
<input type="text" defaultValue="start" />
```

KEY POINTS
- Controlled = state + value + onChange with event.target.value.
- Uncontrolled = no value (maybe defaultValue); the browser manages the text.
- value without onChange makes a read-only input, and React warns about it.

lessons.title: Multi-field forms
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS A form with several inputs can keep one state per field (simple for small forms) or one state object for the whole form with a shared handleChange (better for big forms). With the object, each input needs a name attribute that matches its key. KEY IDEAS 1. One state per field: each input has its own value and setter. Easy to drop {label}, {tier} anywhere. 2. One object: one handler for every input. 3. [name]: value is a computed key. If the input's name is "tier", it updates the tier field. 4. ...prev copies every other field so they aren't lost. CODE One state per field: ```jsx const [name, setName] = useState(''); const [weapon, setWeapon] = useState(''); const [tier, setTier] = useState(''); const [label, setLabel] = useState(''); setName(e.target.value)} /> setWeapon(e.target.value)} /> setTier(e.target.value)} /> setLabel(e.target.value)} />

Name: {name}

Weapon: {weapon}

Tier: {tier}

Label: {label}

``` One object for the form: ```jsx const [treasure, setTreasure] = useState({ name: '', weapon: '', tier: '', label: '' }); function handleChange(event) { const { name, value } = event.target; setTreasure(prevTreasure => ({ ...prevTreasure, // copy name, weapon, tier, label [name]: value // overwrite only the field that was typed in })); } ``` KEY POINTS - Small form (2–5 fields) → one state per field. - Bigger form → one object, setForm(prev => ({ ...prev, [name]: value })). - Each object-form input: name="fieldName" value={form.fieldName} onChange={handleChange}.

Inspect React with the dev tools
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS React Developer Tools is a browser extension that adds a Components tab to DevTools. It shows the component tree and, for the selected component, its props, its state (hooks) and which component rendered it. KEY IDEAS 1. Install React Developer Tools in Chrome, open the app, press F12, and open the Components tab. 2. Left side: the component tree (App → FeedbackForm, EnemySpawnerForm, EnemyList). 3. Right side, for the selected component: - props: data from the parent - hooks/state: data the component owns - rendered by: the parent component and the source file and line 4. Ownership rule: if two siblings need the same data, the state belongs in their parent. STEPS Debugging with DevTools: 1. Open the Components tab. 2. Select the component you expect to change. 3. Look at its state and props. 4. Do the action (click, type). 5. Read the result: - State doesn't change → the bug is in the event handler or the state update. - State changes but the UI doesn't → the bug is in the JSX or CSS. - The state is in a child but a sibling needs it → lift the state up to the parent. CODE ```jsx // App.jsx import EnemySpawnerForm from "./components/EnemySpawnerForm"; import EnemyList from "./components/EnemyList";

Enemy Spawner Form
; } // src/components/EnemyList.jsx export default function EnemyList() { return
Enemy List
; } ``` KEY POINTS - Example seen in class: FeedbackForm's state updated live while typing, which shows the input and state were in sync. - Next step for this project: App owns enemies, EnemySpawnerForm calls onAddEnemy, and EnemyList receives enemies as a prop (Lesson 10).
